meta.title: Graph RAG
meta.thesis: Graph RAG is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A product-support assistant needs to connect customers, products, incidents, and policies across documents. By the end, they should be able to build or review Graph RAG design with entity extraction, relationships, and retrieval paths, measure multi-hop questions answered with explicit evidence paths, and catch the failure where entity extraction errors create confident but wrong graph connections.

mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Graph RAG helps when the answer depends on relationships spread across sources, not just one semantically similar passage.

modules.title: Relationship questions expose classic RAG limits
modules.sub: Graph RAG begins when isolated passages are not enough.
modules.summary: Graph RAG is for connected evidence, not for every knowledge base.
objectives: Define the retrieval problem Graph RAG solves.
Decide when classic RAG is sufficient.

blocks.title: Some answers live between chunks

spans.text: Problem anchor: an operations lead asks which product features depend on a vendor whose contract is expiring. No single policy page says the full answer. The evidence is spread across architecture notes, vendor docs, feature ownership pages, and incident records.
Classic vector search can retrieve related chunks, but it may not connect vendor, service, feature, team, and incident into a defensible chain. Graph RAG makes those connections retrievable.
If the answer needs “A depends on B because C owns D,” list the entities and relations before choosing a retriever.

blocks.analogy: Classic RAG finds pages; Graph RAG can follow the index cards pinned between them.

spans.text: The corpus contains docs for AuthFlow, Billing, VendorX, and incident postmortems. A graph extracts nodes for services, vendors, teams, and incidents, with edges such as DEPENDS_ON, OWNS, and MENTIONED_IN.

A query for “What breaks if VendorX sunsets the embeddings endpoint?” seeds VendorX, expands to dependent services, then retrieves source chunks for each edge. The final answer cites paths, not only passages.

items.text: Extract candidate entities from each chunk.
Store edges with source chunk IDs and confidence.
Resolve aliases such as “VendorX API” and “VX embeddings.”
At query time, retrieve seed entities and expand a bounded neighborhood.

blocks.title: Graph fit
blocks.prompt: Which question most clearly calls for Graph RAG?

options.text: What is the refund deadline in the billing policy?
Which teams and features are indirectly affected by VendorX through shared services?
Summarize the introduction paragraph of one document.

blocks.explanation: The affected-features question depends on relationships across multiple sources.

modules.title: Entities and edges need provenance
modules.sub: A graph claim must point back to source text.
modules.summary: Graph structure is useful only when every important edge can be audited.
objectives: Describe entity extraction and edge extraction.
Explain why entity resolution is hard.
Attach source provenance to graph claims.

blocks.title: Edges are evidence claims

spans.text: An LLM-extracted edge like “Billing DEPENDS_ON VendorX” is a claim, not a fact by itself. It needs source chunk IDs, extraction date, confidence, and ideally the exact sentence or table row that supported it.

Entity resolution is a major failure point. “OpenAI,” “Open AI,” and “the model vendor” may refer to the same entity in one corpus and different entities in another. Bad merges poison graph traversal.
For each high-impact edge, ask whether a reviewer can open the source and verify it in under a minute.

blocks.analogy: A graph edge without provenance is a rumor with a neat label.

spans.text: A source chunk says “Billing uses VendorX embeddings to classify invoice disputes.” The graph stores Service:Billing, Vendor:VendorX, Capability:invoice dispute classification, and an edge Billing USES VendorX with the source chunk ID.
At answer time, the generated explanation cites the source chunk behind the edge, not the graph database alone. If the source changes, the edge can be re-extracted or retired.

items.text: Extract entities and proposed relations from chunks.
Normalize aliases with human-reviewed rules for critical entities.
Store source chunk IDs and spans on edges.
Use edge provenance in the answer context.

blocks.title: Provenance check
blocks.prompt: Why should an extracted graph edge keep a source chunk ID?

options.text: So the LLM can ignore document permissions.
So generated answers and audits can verify the relationship against original evidence.
So vector search is no longer needed.

blocks.explanation: Graph structure complements source evidence; it does not replace it.

modules.title: Query planning chooses vector, graph, or both
modules.sub: Graph RAG is an orchestration choice at query time.
modules.summary: The query should decide how much graph expansion is warranted.
objectives: Seed graph traversal from query entities or retrieved chunks.
Bound hop count and relationship types.
Combine vector evidence with graph neighborhoods.

blocks.title: Start with seeds, then expand deliberately

spans.text: A graph query usually needs seed entities. Seeds can come from entity linking in the user question, vector retrieval over entity descriptions, or classic retrieval over chunks that mention candidate entities.
Expansion should be bounded: max hops, allowed edge types, freshness filters, and source permissions. Otherwise the graph can wander into weakly related neighborhoods and flood the prompt.
If a graph expansion adds context, name the relationship that made each added item relevant.

blocks.analogy: Graph traversal is a guided walk, not a sightseeing tour.

cells.text: Retrieve chunks directly by semantic similarity.
Link entities, expand edges, retrieve provenance.

options.name: Vector seeds plus graph expansion

cells.text: Use retrieved chunks to find seed entities, then expand.
Bad first-stage retrieval biases the graph walk.

options.whenToUse: Use when entity names are implicit.

blocks.title: Query plan
blocks.prompt: A user asks for the refund deadline in one policy page. What should the system likely do?

options.text: Run community detection for every query.
Use classic retrieval first; graph traversal is probably unnecessary.
Extract new graph edges during answer generation only.

blocks.explanation: Graph RAG is a tool for relationship-heavy questions, not a default for all lookup.

modules.title: Implement a bounded graph expansion
modules.sub: Small traversal code reveals hop and edge-type behavior.
modules.summary: Graph RAG needs explicit limits that traces can show.
objectives: Represent edges with type and provenance.
Expand from seed entities with max hops.
Predict which nodes and chunks enter context.

spans.text: Max hops, edge types, confidence thresholds, and provenance filters are as important as vector top-k. They decide what the generator can see.
Spaced recall: from chunking, source chunk IDs still matter. Graph expansion should bring back the text behind edges, not just node names.
Print the path that led each evidence chunk into the prompt. If the path is not meaningful, do not include it.

blocks.title: Bounded relationship expansion
blocks.explanation: The traversal returns paths and source chunk IDs, which are the minimum ingredients needed to assemble grounded answer context.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before running it, predict which feature node appears because VendorX is used by Billing.
predictThenReveal.answer: InvoiceDisputes appears through VendorX -> Billing -> InvoiceDisputes, and the trace keeps the source chunk behind each edge.

blocks.title: Traversal guardrail
blocks.prompt: What should happen when graph expansion reaches a node through an irrelevant edge type?

options.text: Let the model decide silently after seeing it.
Filter it out before it becomes answer context.

blocks.explanation: Edge-type filters keep traversal aligned with the user’s relationship question.

modules.title: Graph answers fail through false edges
modules.sub: Evaluation must inspect paths, not only final prose.
modules.summary: Graph RAG quality depends on extraction, resolution, traversal, and synthesis.
objectives: Verify answer claims against source-backed paths.
Decide when a human review gate is needed.

blocks.title: The graph can hallucinate before the model does

spans.text: Graph RAG adds new failure modes: false extracted edges, duplicate entity merges, stale relationships, over-broad community summaries, and path expansion that looks connected but does not answer the question.
Evaluation should ask: Did the system choose the right seed? Were the traversed edges correct? Did the answer cite the source behind each relationship? Did the model overstate a weak path?
For high-impact operational answers, require the output to show path evidence or defer to human review.

blocks.title: Verify AI output from Graph RAG

spans.text: Inspect both graph evidence and final language.

items.text: Each relationship claim maps to a source-backed edge or source chunk.
Entity aliases are resolved correctly for the domain and time period.
The graph path answers the question rather than merely connecting related nodes.
Community summaries are backed by retrievable source evidence.
The answer distinguishes confirmed paths from uncertain or missing relationships.

blocks.title: Graph faithfulness
blocks.prompt: The answer says Feature A depends on VendorX, but the path only shows both mentioned in one incident summary. What is wrong?

options.text: The answer is safe because graph paths always imply causality.
The relationship is overstated; co-mention is not dependency evidence.
The model should remove all citations.

blocks.explanation: Graph paths need semantically valid edge types and source support.

rag.label: RAG
rag.laymanDefinition: Retrieving relevant evidence before generation so answers can be grounded in sources.
rag.technicalNote: RAG quality depends on corpus freshness, chunking, embeddings, filters, ranking, citation handling, and faithfulness evaluation.

embedding.label: Embedding
embedding.laymanDefinition: A numeric vector representation of text used for semantic comparison.
embedding.technicalNote: Embedding choices fix dimension, distance metric, query/passage formatting, model version, and migration requirements for retrieval.

vector_search.label: Vector search
vector_search.laymanDefinition: Finding nearby vectors to retrieve semantically related chunks.
vector_search.technicalNote: Vector search needs metadata filters, recall tests, index tuning, and fallback for exact terms, IDs, and rare phrases.

chunk.label: Chunk
chunk.laymanDefinition: A source text segment stored and retrieved as a unit.
chunk.technicalNote: Chunk design balances semantic completeness, citation accuracy, token budget, overlap, metadata, and update/delete behavior.

reranker.label: Reranker
reranker.laymanDefinition: A second-stage model or method that reorders retrieved candidates by relevance.
reranker.technicalNote: Rerankers improve top-result precision when candidate recall is adequate, but add latency, cost, and evaluation complexity.

rrf.label: RRF
rrf.laymanDefinition: A rank-fusion method that merges multiple result lists by reciprocal rank.
rrf.technicalNote: RRF is useful for hybrid retrieval because it combines lexical and vector rankings without requiring comparable raw scores.

questions.q: Does the question require entities, paths, communities, contradictions, or ownership relationships across documents?
questions.why: Graph extraction adds cost and refresh complexity, so it should be reserved for relationship-heavy retrieval failures.
questions.rot: Use Graph RAG when relationship traversal or path explanation is central; use simpler retrieval when one or two passages answer the question.
